about.lead: I’m a <primary>Senior React Frontend Developer</primary> based in Tychy, Poland. I have been building web applications for over 10 years, and since 2019 I have specialised commercially in React and TypeScript, mostly in media products.
body: I work best when I own a piece of the product end to end: from talking through requirements, through architectural decisions, to deployment and maintenance. I like work that cleans up the foundations, such as extracting shared code or merging an app’s state, because only then can new features ship quickly without fear of regressions.

I work closely with the back end, the product owner, design and the people who use what I build every day. I treat code review as a conversation about the solution, and on larger pieces of work I split tasks across the team and help less experienced developers.

I treat AI as a tool, not an autopilot. I work with coding agents every day: I write my own skills and instructions for them based on project conventions, while I keep the architecture and code consistent and review everything they generate.
I try out what’s new in Next.js and React after hours in my own project, [dociekai.pl](https://dociekai.pl), so I talk about changes in the ecosystem from experience, not from changelogs.
I started out as a graphic designer, so I have an eye for UI and get along well with designers.

text: My own project, which I build on my own from idea to deployment: an educational platform with interactive 4th-grade courses (maths, computer science, history, Polish), games, flashcards and quizzes. This is where I keep trying out new versions of Next.js and React.
sideProject.stack: Next.js (App Router, RSC), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind, Strapi, Node.js (API routes), Playwright

items.name: Video and radio players for ZPR Media websites
items.context: Grupa ZPR Media · Multimedia team (9 people) · 2024–present
items.role: Senior React Frontend Developer, owning the team’s entire front end: moving the players into a dedicated repository, architecture decisions, refactoring and rollout, leading the team’s developers on larger front-end work
items._todo: TODO(Moon): sprawdzić opis problemu; liczby ZPR (facts) odświeżać raz na jakiś czas; wizualizacje playerów to mockupy w kodzie (VideoPlayerMock), bez zrzutów ze stagingu
items.problem: The video and radio players were woven into the code of each of the group’s websites. Every fix meant deployments in many places, and ads, analytics and error handling worked slightly differently on every site.
product: The video player is embedded with a single script and a tag with data-* attributes. It plays HLS streams and supports preroll ads, up-next videos, sticky mode, LIVE broadcasts with a scheduled end, and vertical reels with a feed for the newsroom. AutoMatch mode picks a video to match the article’s content on its own.

The radio player streams the group’s stations live (Eska, Eska Rock, Vox FM, Radio Plus and more), fetches “now playing” and the current show from the API, and blocks switching stations while an ad is playing. It has separate desktop and mobile variants.
text: I moved the players out of the websites into a separate React and TypeScript repository, with a single build and CDN deployment process. Websites get a ready-made script and embed code instead of their own copies of the player.
Refactoring of video, audio, radio (live streaming) and podcast players, Google IMA and VAST ad integrations, and Gemius analytics.

Demo pages for presentations and testing: a settings panel generates embed code for the current configuration, and MSW mocks simulate API errors and missing third-party scripts (IMA, HLS, video.js), so every player state can be checked.
E2E tests in Playwright. Beyond the players: React CMS modules for managing radio apps, and article audio based on text-to-speech.

facts.label: internet users a month on the group’s websites where the players run, and 183 million page views
Poles listen to the group’s radio stations every week

items.name: Content editor for the Wirtualna Polska newsroom
items.context: Wirtualna Polska · large back-office tools front-end team · 2022–2024
items.role: React Frontend Developer in the WP team (contract via Autentika), 09.2022–07.2024: from requirements analysis to release, in close cooperation with backend
items._todo: TODO(Moon): liczby wkładu z historii repo n2cr-frontend (stan 31.07.2024); celowo bez nazw wewnętrznych (Corgi, N2CR, Szwadron) i numerów ticketów; potwierdzić, że Scrollytelling dał redakcji format niemożliwy wcześniej
items.problem: The editor was built around a flat list of content blocks, and its state was split between two separate Redux stores, connected by hand-made bridges of middleware and callbacks. New editorial formats, such as multi-column scrollytelling stories, required changes to the very foundation of the app without breaking more than 40 existing templates.
product: The editor is WP journalists’ main tool, part of an ecosystem of back-office apps built on a shared Design System. Newsrooms use it to create and publish articles, galleries, liveblogs, product tests and special features, and each type has its own template and validation.

Articles are assembled from ready-made blocks: images, videos, galleries, quotes, tables, embeds and timelines. The editor suggests images, links and tags based on the content (AI/ML), scores readability and shows a preview of the article in the portal layout.
text: I designed and built the Scrollytelling template from scratch, the most complex one in the editor: a tree-shaped content structure (containers, sections with up to 4 columns, nesting at any depth) in an app built for a flat list of blocks. It gave the newsroom multi-column special features that could not be put together in the editor before, and on the same foundation I built the Binder template, which combines several stories into one publication. This covered the data model, API adapters (a tree on read, a flat list on save), editing logic in sagas and reducers, the UI, validation and integration tests.

I merged two independent Redux stores, the app’s and the editor’s, into one. The hand-made bridges between them are gone, and the app has a single source of truth. This unblocked the next milestone in the editor’s development: refactoring its core text-editing library, which had kept running into the split state. For the newsroom the change was invisible: the editor worked exactly as before.

Editor performance: I split embeds into separate components (social media, Infogram, Typeform) that load their iframes only once they enter the viewport, and removed layout shift of content blocks on load.

A dozen or so new templates and content types that widened what the newsroom can prepare in the editor, including consumer tests with results and validation, car tests and author bios, plus X, Telegram, Reels and Spotify embeds and hotspots on gallery images.
Integrating the editor with WP’s website builder platform: role-based permissions and UI restrictions, and a proxy to an external API as a new Nx library with Next.js API routes.
CI/CD: I extended the GitLab CI pipelines to two data centres and rewrote the deployment script from Python to TypeScript (zx, argument validation with zod).

Unit, integration and E2E tests (Jest, React Testing Library, Cypress) and code review in an NX monorepo. The team of a tech lead, developers and juniors had a flat structure: we designed the architecture together, and I helped my teammates, especially junior developers.

facts.label: articles in the database, thousands of tags, hundreds of authors
new templates and content types for the newsroom, including multi-column Scrollytelling
Redux stores merged into one, unblocking the refactor of the editor’s core text-editing library
existing templates kept working unchanged after the foundations were rebuilt

items.name: A data search app with a GIS map for geologists
items.role: React Frontend Developer (contract via Autentika), 11.2021–05.2022: the map, layers panel, filters and design system components
items._todo: TODO(Moon): treść z historii repo kadme (gałąź development, 24.11.2021–11.05.2022); nazwa produktu (Lumin) celowo pominięta – publicznie potwierdzone jest tylko Kadme (case study Autentiki); potwierdzić, czy @kadme/components można podawać publicznie
items.problem: The map was the heart of the app, but the React wrapper over OpenLayers (rlayers) gave no access to the low-level features the design called for: a terrain basemap in brand colours instead of the standard tile palette, and custom handling of layers, menus and points on the map.
product: Kadme’s app is a “mapplication” for geologists and field specialists: the map is at its centre, alongside a search engine for unstructured data from many sources, with filters, source previews and search history. Before, every search depended on data managers being available.

Data layers are overlaid on the map and show only what is relevant to the current search. The app runs in the office and on rugged tablets on drilling platforms, and its components were built in isolation in Storybook, in parallel with the UI design.
text: I moved the map from the rlayers wrapper to the native OpenLayers 6 API in all of its views: main, mini and modal. On that foundation I built the layers panel and the interactions: interactive points, a layer context menu, a coordinates popup and animated zoom.
Colourised terrain basemap: tiles go through a RasterSource that converts every pixel from RGB to the HCL colour space and back, repainting the terrain in the app’s palette.
Layers panel: layers from GeoJSON data (polygons with labels and styles), field groups with a visibility toggle and a slider, plus new SwitchField and RangeInput components in the design system.

The @kadme/components design system: I rebuilt about 10 base components to match new Figma designs (including Button, Tooltip, Popover and Tile) and added 6 new ones, including Tabs, FAB and SourceBrowser – a three-level data source tree with a custom scrollbar, built from scratch. Every component had a Storybook story and went through code review.

In the app: a filters sidebar with a mobile version, connected to the widget usage modal (I made more commits to filters than the rest of the team combined), layout views, a settings modal and bookmarks, results rendering fixes, and a batch of fixes after acceptance testing.

outcomes.title: A map free of wrapper limits
outcomes.text: Moving to native OpenLayers unlocked the features the design called for, which the wrapper gave no access to.

outcomes.title: Terrain in brand colours
outcomes.text: The basemap matches the rest of the interface instead of standing out with the standard tile palette.

outcomes.title: Ready-made components for the team
outcomes.text: A design system aligned with the new Figma designs and documented in Storybook: new views were assembled from ready-made components.

outcomes.title: Filters on mobile too
outcomes.text: Search is narrowed by filters connected to the widgets, which also work on smaller screens.

items.name: dociekai.pl – interactive courses for 4th grade
items.role: Sole author: idea, product design, architecture, front end and lesson content. AI agents (Claude Code) write much of the code; I lead them as a tech lead and review every change.
items.problem: Learning materials for pupils are mostly texts and videos. I wanted courses that follow the 4th-grade core curriculum, where a child learns by doing and the page grades every task itself, with no answer key.

decisions.title: A shared lesson engine for four courses
decisions.text: A lesson is a list of blocks on a shared shell that handles progress, completion and the learning streak. A course only supplies its own widgets and grading functions. The same engine runs, among others, a spreadsheet with a formula parser, a Scratch-style editor and stage, historical maps, a timeline and a family tree.

decisions.title: Grading as pure functions, covered by self-tests
decisions.text: The logic that grades a child’s answer lives outside React. 55 self-test suites (esbuild + Node) cover cases you can’t sensibly click through. The family tree doesn’t say “wrong”; it points to the two people who contradict each other.

decisions.title: Progress without an account, merged into it after sign-up
decisions.text: Every lesson works fully without an account. After sign-up, progress from the session is merged into the account. Sync is deferred and doesn’t block learning when the network fails. One implementation serves all four courses.

decisions.title: A learning streak counted in school days
decisions.text: I store only raw “day → lessons”. The streak, the record, freezes and 24 badges are derived by pure functions. Weekends, public holidays and school breaks cost nothing. Merging across devices is a union of day sets, so sync order doesn’t matter and nothing is lost.

decisions.title: Static-first, resilient to CMS outages
decisions.text: Next.js App Router, with data from the Strapi headless CMS fetched at build time. The browser talks only to my own API routes, which return empty data instead of a page error when something fails. Sign-in (email, Google, JWT) goes only through a proxy on the Next.js side.

decisions.title: A custom Cloudinary loader instead of Vercel’s optimiser
decisions.text: I bypassed Vercel’s image optimiser with a custom Cloudinary loader, because per-transformation billing was eating up the quota. Images are addressed by keys with a local fallback, and a pre-commit hook blocks heavy binaries.

details.title: One task, from data to lesson
blocks: In a history lesson about family, the child places a made-up family on the shelves of a family tree, one shelf per generation.

steps: Data: a list of people with their birth year and parents. There is no answer key.

Judge: a pure function derives the correct shelves from two rules (a child stands one shelf above their parents, spouses share a shelf). Instead of giving the answer away, it names the two people who contradict each other and gives their years.
Self-test: the judge is tested without React and without a browser.
Widget: handles only drawing and interaction, on a shared drag hook with a “tap and place” variant.
Lesson: a list of blocks passed to the course shell.

blocks: In another lesson the same engine handles the family of the Greek gods. There are no dates there, so the shelves follow from kinship alone.

images.alt: The Lisiecki family tree task on desktop: people to place, shelves from trunk to crown and two messages saying Józef and his children stand two levels apart
The same task on a 390 px wide phone: the tray of people, the tree shelves and the contradiction messages stacked one below another

details.title: How I work with AI agents
blocks: I decide what gets built and how, and agents get small, bounded tasks with documented conventions, a reference file and a clear definition of done. I hand simple mechanics to cheaper models. I keep architecture, widget and grading logic, the texts for children and review for myself. I check most closely the places where a bug costs most: state that is saved and synced, and the logic that tells a ten-year-old whether they got it right. Nothing goes in without typecheck, lint and self-tests.
The guardrails are the ones that would let a team scale: strict TypeScript, tested grading functions, Playwright on desktop and mobile, CI on every push, shared lesson shells.

list: Move the JWT from localStorage to an httpOnly cookie. Reading the token already lives in one module, and I sanitise the blog HTML on the server.
Some drag widgets aren’t fully keyboard-operable. The fix for the shared hook sits in one place.
E2E coverage is thin. Correctness rests mainly on self-tests, and the widgets deserve component tests.
A few widgets are close to 1000 lines. To be split into a reducer, a view and content.
The new React Compiler rules run as warnings for now (about 200 places that predate them). I’m migrating gradually.

facts.label: 4th-grade courses: maths, computer science, history, Polish
interactive lessons and 16 guides; three courses complete, Polish in progress (18 of 48)
self-test suites for grading, streak and sanitiser logic; run in CI on every push
Lighthouse score in every category, performance included, on desktop and mobile
